\section{Experiments}

\subsection{Setup}

We test these predictions on synthetic and semi-synthetic data generating processes (DGPs); full specifications appear in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.
The synthetic DGP generates $N{=}5{,}000$ observations from a randomized trial with $K \in \{2, 4\}$ subgroups, controlled CATE heterogeneity $\Delta\tau$, and subgroup-specific symmetric misclassification rates with heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$.
Expert labels ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{50, \ldots, 2000\}$) are a simple random sample with true $Z$ observed; each configuration is repeated for 100 Monte Carlo runs.
The semi-synthetic DGP samples $N{=}5{,}000$ tweets from TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, defining $K{=}4$ subgroups by crossing hashtag presence and text length (unbalanced: 39\%/38\%/12\%/11\%), with misclassification rates $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$ reflecting empirical evidence that text features degrade LLM accuracy~\cite{ashwin2025bias}.

We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix, equivalent to PPI/DSL~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,egami2024dsl} with homogeneous error), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup DSL without shrinkage), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
Robustness validation covers hate speech detection ($\Delta\pi{=}0.117$; Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}), six OpenAI models (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm}), subgroup misspecification ($\geq$94.5\% coverage at 50\% noise; Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}), and asymmetric confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{app:semireal}).

\subsection{Empirical Validation of the Bias Identity}
\label{sec:bias_mechanism}

The bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) predicts that global correction introduces bias proportional to $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ at the subgroup level.
We verify this identity on a $K{=}2$ parameter grid of 520 configurations spanning 26 misclassification heterogeneity levels ($\Delta\pi \in [0, 0.25]$) and 20 CATE heterogeneity levels ($\Delta\tau \in (0, 0.50]$), and separately on a $K{=}4$ grid (Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}).
Regressing observed subgroup bias on the Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} prediction ($\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1{-}2\bar{\pi})$) yields $R^2 = 0.994$ for $K{=}2$ and $R^2 = 0.974$ for $K{=}4$; the residual variance reflects MC sampling noise rather than model misspecification, since Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is an exact identity at the population level ($R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$; Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}).
Global correction worsens CATE bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta\pi{=}0$ rows) across our parameter grid---concentrated in regimes where $\Delta\pi > 0.10$ and per-subgroup expert samples exceed 25---consistent with Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}.
Maximum observed amplification reaches 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 2.41$\times$ ($K{=}4$) relative to the naive estimator.
Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ amplification surface across the $K{=}2$ parameter grid.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig2_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Bias amplification under global correction across the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ parameter grid ($K{=}2$). (a) Low-error subgroup: global correction always helps (ratio $< 1$). (b) High-error subgroup: when $\Delta\pi > 0.12$ (dashed line), global correction \emph{increases} bias relative to the naive estimator (hatched region), with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$.}
\label{fig:heatmap}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{EC-HTE Evaluation}
\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
Notably, in the $K{=}2$ extreme row, global correction \emph{increases} $|\text{bias}|$ relative to naive (0.059 vs.\ 0.058)---a direct manifestation of Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}: pooled correction overshoots in low-error subgroups.
HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 (global) to 0.010 (a 5.9$\times$ reduction) while maintaining nominal coverage (0.95) and comparable RMSE (0.093 vs.\ 0.099).
The advantage persists at $K{=}4$: EC-HTE achieves $|\text{bias}|{=}0.008$ versus 0.056 for global (7.0$\times$ reduction), though with a small RMSE penalty (0.126 vs.\ 0.125).
Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), methods converge: EC-HTE and global achieve comparable bias ($p > 0.05$; Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}).
In the semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K{=}4$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$), EC-HTE and Global achieve comparable $|\text{bias}|$ (0.027 vs.\ 0.023, $p{=}0.395$; Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}), but EC-HTE incurs higher aggregate RMSE (0.225 vs.\ 0.124), driven by moderate $\Delta\pi{=}0.20$, highly unbalanced subgroups (12\%/11\% receiving ${\sim}30$ expert labels each), and RMSE degradation in small subgroups where noisy $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ estimation dominates (S3: 0.480 vs.\ 0.145).
EC-HTE's advantage requires both sufficient $\Delta\pi$ and adequate per-subgroup expert budget; when either is marginal, global correction is competitive on aggregate RMSE.

\paragraph{CausalForest.}
With CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal} as the downstream estimator ($K{=}4$, extreme, $n{=}500$), EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 to 0.040 (4.8$\times$) with coverage improvement from 0.58 to 0.91 (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
The debiasing-hurts phenomenon intensifies---global correction amplifies naive bias by up to 5.9$\times$---because the forest's sensitivity to covariate noise magnifies label errors.
Oracle experiments (true $Z$, no correction) confirm CausalForest plug-in SE is well-calibrated (94--96\% coverage); the residual aggregate coverage gap (83--85\% in some regimes) reflects asymmetric $M^{-1}$ SE propagation across subgroups, not confusion matrix estimation uncertainty ($<$2\% of total variance at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$; Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
Budget requirements are stricter (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Main results under extreme misclassification heterogeneity. $|\text{Bias}|$ and RMSE averaged over subgroups, $z$-levels, and 100 MC runs. Bold marks lowest $|\text{bias}|$ per block. $^\dagger$RMSE exceeds Global, reflecting stratification variance cost. Additional configurations (moderate heterogeneity, semi-synthetic TweetEval) in Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}. MC standard errors: Appendix~\ref{app:mcse}.}
\label{tab:main_results}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
\begin{tabular}{ll ccc}
\toprule
Configuration & Method & $|\text{Bias}|$ & RMSE & Cov. \\
\midrule
\multirow{4}{*}{\shortstack[l]{DIM\\$K{=}2$, $n{=}250$}}
 & Naive & 0.058 & 0.090 & 0.82 \\
 & Global & 0.059 & 0.099 & 0.87 \\
 & Strat.\ MLE & 0.012 & 0.094 & 0.95 \\
 & HB EC-HTE & \textbf{0.010} & 0.093 & 0.95 \\
\midrule
\multirow{4}{*}{\shortstack[l]{DIM\\$K{=}4$, $n{=}500$}}
 & Naive & 0.062 & 0.113 & 0.88 \\
 & Global & 0.056 & 0.125 & 0.91 \\
 & Strat.\ MLE & 0.010 & 0.127$^\dagger$ & 0.95 \\
 & HB EC-HTE & \textbf{0.008} & 0.126$^\dagger$ & 0.95 \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{\shortstack[l]{CausalForest\\$K{=}4$, $n{=}500$}}
 & Naive & 0.208 & 0.231 & 0.44 \\
 & Global & 0.191 & 0.244 & 0.58 \\
 & EC-HTE Forest & \textbf{0.040} & 0.224 & 0.91 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\subsection{Actionable Diagnostic Without EC-HTE}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction increases bias in subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, where $\delta_s = \pi_s - \bar{\pi}$.
Since this depends only on misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample, practitioners can flag harmful correction before estimating any treatment effects.
A threshold classifier achieves AUC = 0.86 at the subgroup level (0.89 at the setting level), outperforming $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ (AUC = 0.73) which requires unobservable CATE heterogeneity (Figure~\ref{fig:roc}, Appendix).
On real LLM confusion matrices (16 model--dataset combinations, Appendix~\ref{app:screening}), the pooled diagnostic AUC decreases to 0.63, primarily because real classifiers exhibit asymmetric FPR/FNR ratios (e.g., 7:1) that violate~(A2).
For $K{=}2$ subgroups, $|\delta_0|{=}|\delta_1|$ causes the diagnostic to rank subgroups solely by $1/\pi_s$, which can anti-predict actual harm.
The diagnostic is most reliable for $K{\geq}4$ with moderate error-rate asymmetry.

\paragraph{Recommended workflow.}
Practitioners should (i) collect $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 25K / P(Z_{\text{minority}})$ stratified expert labels, (ii) verify per-subgroup budget $\geq 25$, $\max(\text{FPR}, \text{FNR}) < 0.5$, and $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) \leq 100$ (Section~\ref{sec:method}), (iii) evaluate the diagnostic (Equation~\ref{eq:hurts_condition}), and (iv) apply EC-HTE when flagged; PPCI can be composed for outcome error (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).
Budget crossover curves and diagnostic screening of 11 real LLM confusion matrices appear in Appendices~\ref{sec:budget}--\ref{app:screening}.

We further validate the bias identity across eight LLMs spanning 11 model--dataset combinations ($R^2 = 0.975$; Appendix~\ref{app:multilm}).

With CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal} as the downstream estimator ($K{=}4$, extreme, $n{=}500$), EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 to 0.040 (4.8$\times$) with coverage improvement from 0.58 to 0.91 (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
The debiasing-hurts phenomenon intensifies---global correction amplifies naive bias by up to 5.9$\times$---because the forest's sensitivity to covariate noise magnifies label errors.
Oracle experiments (true $Z$, no correction) confirm CausalForest plug-in SE is well-calibrated (94--96\% coverage); the residual aggregate coverage gap (83--85\% in some regimes) reflects asymmetric $M^{-1}$ SE propagation across subgroups, not confusion matrix estimation uncertainty ($<$2\% of total variance at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$; Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
Budget requirements are stricter (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).

\subsection{Actionable Diagnostic Without EC-HTE}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction increases bias in subgroup $s$ iff $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, computable from a pilot sample without estimating treatment effects.
A threshold classifier achieves AUC = 0.86 (subgroup level; 0.89 setting level), outperforming $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ (AUC = 0.73; Figure~\ref{fig:roc}, Appendix).
On real LLM confusion matrices (16 model--dataset combinations, Appendix~\ref{app:screening}), the pooled diagnostic AUC decreases to 0.63, primarily because real classifiers exhibit asymmetric FPR/FNR ratios (e.g., 7:1) that violate~(A2).
For $K{=}2$ subgroups, $|\delta_0|{=}|\delta_1|$ causes the diagnostic to rank subgroups solely by $1/\pi_s$, which can anti-predict actual harm.
The diagnostic is most reliable for $K{\geq}4$ with moderate error-rate asymmetry.

\paragraph{Recommended workflow.}
Practitioners should (i) collect $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 25K / P(Z_{\text{minority}})$ stratified expert labels, (ii) verify per-subgroup budget $\geq 25$, $\max(\text{FPR}, \text{FNR}) < 0.5$, and $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) \leq 100$ (Section~\ref{sec:method}), (iii) evaluate the diagnostic (Equation~\ref{eq:hurts_condition}), and (iv) apply EC-HTE when flagged; PPCI can be composed for outcome error (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).
Budget crossover curves and diagnostic screening of 11 real LLM confusion matrices appear in Appendices~\ref{sec:budget}--\ref{app:screening}.

We further validate the bias identity across eight LLMs spanning 11 model--dataset combinations ($R^2 = 0.975$; Appendix~\ref{app:multilm}).
